newsitem.title: HUNGARY: CENTRAL/EAST EUROPEAN STOCKS HAVE BUOYANT WEEK.
newsitem.headline: CENTRAL/EAST EUROPEAN STOCKS HAVE BUOYANT WEEK.

text.p: Friday's drops on the Warsaw
and Budapest stock exchange chopped away at gains made earlier
this week, while Prague hit a record high on Friday and
Bratislava also rose.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which reflects
price movements in 73 Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Slovak and
Slovenian stocks, firmed 1.67 percent over the week to close at
a new record high of 1,739.06 points.
PRAGUE
Spectacular gains for the PX50's biggest banking issue,
Komercni Banka, spurred the index on to a string of 12-month
highs with dealers seeing room for further advances in the
coming sessions.
"It's the psychology of the mass (group). Our analysts
predict further increases in the next months," said Petr
Opocensky of Citicorp Securities in Prague.
Komercni, which has risen by around 15 percent since the
beginning of the week, was pushed up by strong long term
arbitrage possibilities existing between Komercni's price on
the Prague bourse, 3,050 at Friday's close, and its global
depositary receipt price in London, currently 3,398.
WARSAW
The Warsaw Stock Exchange eased 0.2 percent this week,
setting a 35-month high on Tuesday and analysts expected it to
fall in profit-taking, possibly next week, after having gained
about 38 percent since mid-December.
"All ratios of technical analysis are overheated and show
sell-signals, companies earnings reports for January were not
spectacular, so surely the correction will happen," said Pawel
Dmytryk, a trader at Bank Staropolski brokerage.
Some analysts said the expected profit-taking correction
could last about a month and was likely to pull the WIG index
down to 16,000 points.
But they said Poland's good economic prospects and
expanding possibilities such as new issues and forthcoming
large privatisations were attracting new, foreign capital,
which could later push the WIG index up.
BUDAPEST
Hungarian share prices edged lower through the week as
Friday's losses chopped mild gains off the week after
bourse-listed companies completed the publication of their
preliminary 1996 earnings reports. On Friday the BUX index
finished at 5,510.36 points, down 0.19 from last Friday.
"The market reached the end of an expansive period and
investors will now review what to invest in," one trader said.
The share market has calmed down and investors were waiting
for the planned new phase of a selloff in oil company MOL.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) extended last week's
uptrend with four consecutive year highs this week. Brokers
said the gains may continue due to strong demand for still
undervalued blue chips and high interbank market rates
prompting foreign capital to turn to the stock market.
The 16-share SAX index rose 5.28 points from Monday's
opening, or 2.68 percent, to close at 201.95 points on
Thursday.
"In principle, blue chips are rising and trading has become
more lively as currently higher interbank money market rates
had attracted some foreign capital inflow," Vladimir Kuklis, a
CSOB Bank analyst said. "It appears that the trend will
continue for a while."
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks closed the week mixed with modest trade on
Friday, but dealers predicted most prices would hold ground.
They said current stagnation was caused by the absence of
foreign investors who were turned off by slow ownership
registration.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares firmed 1.1 percent this week, as the
blue-chip SBI index rose 15.63 points to 1,385.03.
Pharmaceuticals trader Salus outperformed the market, rising
14.9 percent, while financial consultancy Primofin bucked the
trend, plummeting 13 percent.
BUCHAREST
Heavy trading in first-tier stocks Azomures SA fertiliser
maker and chemical plant Oltchim SA, which joined the market
on Tuesday, kept turnover on the Bucharest bourse high this
week.
Demand outrunning supply sent the bulk of prices up on
Thursday, when the independent VAB and BIG indices hit year
highs.
TIRANA
For the second consecutive week, neither T-bills (Treasury
bills) nor bonds were traded on the dormant Tirana Stock
Exchange during its two weekly sessions on Monday and Thursday.
"Two banks are really taking care to preserve their
liquidity now since the lek is weakening," said a trader.
The local currency has hit a record low of about 130 leks
to the dollar, having dropped some 25 percent since the start
of the year, as Albania plunged into its biggest political and
financial crisis since the fall of communism six years ago.
The collapse of several fraudulent investment schemes in
January left many Albanians penniless and has stirred up weeks
of popular unrest across the country.
The right-wing government of President Sali Berisha has
promised help to some of the hardest-hit investors, but has
insisted that it would not print money to bail them out.
